sie.et: From Middle High German siu, si, from Old High German siu, si, from Proto-West Germanic *si(j)u, *sī, from Proto-Germanic *sī (see Proto-Germanic *iz). Cognate with Gothic 𐍃𐌹 (si) and Old English sēo f (“that one”).
From Middle High German sie, si (neuter siu), from Old High German sie (masculine plural), sio (feminine plural), siu (neuter plural).

Siebenmeilenstiefel.et: From sieben (“seven”) + Meilen (“miles”) + Stiefel (“boots”). In the German-speaking countries a mile was about 7.5 km (thus roughly 5 international miles).

s: seven (numerical value represented by the Arabic numeral 7; or describing a set with seven elements)

From Middle High German siben, from Old High German sibun, from Proto-West Germanic *sebun, from Proto-Germanic *sebun, from earlier Proto-Germanic *sebunt, from Proto-Indo-European *septḿ̥.
Compare Dutch zeven, English seven.
From Middle High German siben or sieben, likely from Old High German sib (“a sieve”). By surface analysis, Sieb + -en.

sieden.et: From Middle High German sieden, from Old High German siodan, from Proto-Germanic *seuþaną.

siebzehn.et: From Middle High German sibenzehen, from Old High German sibunzehan, from Proto-Germanic *sebuntehun. Equivalent to sieben + zehn. Compare Dutch zeventien, West Frisian santjin, English seventeen, Danish sytten.

siebzig.et: From Middle High German sibenzec, from Old High German sibunzug, from Proto-Germanic *sebuntēhundą. Equivalent to sieben + -zig. Cognate with Hunsrik sibzich.

Siegel.et: From Middle High German sigel and Middle Low German seg(g)el, both from Latin sigillum. Compare Dutch zegel.
From Middle High German sigel and Middle Low German seg(g)el, both from Latin sigillum. Compare Dutch zegel.

Sascha verwirrte Menschen sehr oft, weil sier sich weder als Frau noch als Mann zu erkennen gab.
Sascha confused people very often, because they didn’t present themselves as either a woman or a man.
Da sier weit entfernt von mir wohnt, kann ich einen Besuch bei siem nicht oft machen. Ich vermisse sien so sehr.

Wie kann man Wasser in einem Sieb tragen?

Sieb.et: From Middle High German sip, from Old High German sib, from Proto-West Germanic *sibi. Cognate with Dutch zeef, English sieve.

Sieg.et: From Middle High German sige, sic, from Old High German sigu, sigi, from Proto-West Germanic *sigi, from Proto-Germanic *segaz, from Proto-Indo-European *seǵʰ- (“related to overpowering”).

From Old High German Sigin (whence Medieval Latin Sigina), either from:
* Proto-Indo-European *seǵʰ- (“related to overpowering”), so called after the force of the water, one gush overtaking the other, then cognate to the Schüß / Schüss / Suze f in Bern, Sionge…

a female given name, notably of the mother of Siegfried in German mythology

you see?; didn't I tell you so?

Literally, “may someone look on!”, or more loosely translated as “look at that!”.
